newsitem.title: EGYPT: Egypt starts military trial of 97 men and women.
newsitem.headline: Egypt starts military trial of 97 men and women.

text.p: Egypt on Saturday began the military trial of 97 men and women on charges including forgery, murder and belonging to a Moslem militant group.
The defendants were held in a partitioned cage for the hearing, under tight security with armed guards standing by.
The charges carry sentences from one year in jail for harbouring a fugitive to the death penalty for operating an illegal group or killing, lawyers said.
This is one of the biggest military trials in Egypt and also marks the first time that a military court has tried women.

Halima Khalifa Arafa, 54, her two daughters and two sons are charged with sheltering a suspected militant, who was later killed. The charges against the other two women in the trial include smuggling instructions from prisoners.
The court at Heikstep outside Cairo adjourned until July 9 after the charges were read.
Among the main charges is membership in Al-Gama'a al-Islamiya (Islamic Group), the main militant group fighting to transform Egypt into a strict Islamic state.
Incidents in the case date back to 1994, when bombs exploded outside nine state and private banks and other companies.
The case also covers the killing of police general Raouf Khairat in 1994. Two alleged killers were shot dead by police.
Five of the accused are being tried in their absence. There were originally 98 in the case but lawyers said one defendant died while in custody.
Among the 92 in court was Mohammad Fawzy, who has been sentenced to death in another case and is waiting for the implementation of the verdict. He looked in good spirits.
"It is not just me, but all people here have good morale," Fawzy told Reuters.
All the men were dressed in prison garb. Four of the women wore veils.
The prisoners were mostly silent during the two-hour session. During the break some of them chatted through the bars to relatives, who passed them photographs of their children.
Some defendants have been in detention since 1993 for other cases and have not had visitors, relatives and lawyers said.
The majority were granted bail but authorities kept them detained under an emergency law, lawyers said.
Some were arrested in Saudi Arabia and returned to Egypt.
Defendants complained to Reuters of conditions, saying tuberculosis was rife at Faiyum and New Valley detention camps.
The trial was held under maximum security. A security guard tore out pages of a reporter's notebook when he wrote down statements from a defendant's relatives.
During the break, one of the defendants recited a call from five Gama'a leaders who are in prison to the group's leaders at large to stop all "military operations".
"The unilateral truce is in the interest of Islam and Moslems. I am sure the leaders will fulfill it," he said.
More than 1,000 people have been killed in political violence since the militants took up arms in 1992 to topple the government of President Hosni Mubarak.
